Hiya folks,

I'd appreciate any insights you might have about this.

I built a mini ITX htpc a few months ago, and last week started having some trouble with it. My wife first reported that when she started watching netflix it would reboot. As a typical husband I ignored the problem until it affected me. A few days later it happened to me, I can't remember if it was netflix or hard drive video I/we was/were watching. No shut down, an immediate off and reboot.

It has been unseasonably warm here and this computer usually stays on 24/7 so I reckoned it was probably overheating. I cleared the area around it a bit better (some DVD cases had migrated closer to it than I had ever intended them too) and propped up the front edge of the case with a lego technic beam to let air get under the case and cool it better.I also positioned the living room fan to blow at the case.

Things got much worse. Instead of rebooting once or twice a day, it started to reboot 5-6 times a day.

My google-fu suggested that random reboots could be caused by RAM that needs to be reseated. So the next day before I went to work I opened up the case, dismounted the PSU, and flipped it up out of the way (mini ITX, everything is in the way of everything), carefully removed and reseated the RAM, reassembled the computer, and threw the switch.

Nothing happened. What. the. hell. No BIOS no anything, check power connection, check power bar, everything looks fine.

"maybe I accidentally disconnected the power switch while reseating the RAM", open up the computer again, connector looks fine, but I guess I may as well reseat the switch connector while I've got everything open. TRAP SPRUNG. That connector which combines power switch, power light, HDD light, is actually 3 connectors and now you can't tell which ones go on which pins. Time to leave for work.

Get home, 12 hours later, guesstimate which pins power switch connector should be on, re-assemble computer (no screws yet).

It works. ~48 hours no problems.

What's going on?

Overheating? (weird that it would reboot and not just shutdown and stay off, and that improving airflow aggravated the problem)

RAM? (maybe tilting the computer back on that lego brick worsened the problem because it put a non perpendicular load on the chip?)

PSU? (maybe tilting the computer back on that lego brick worsened the problem because a fan was not resting on its bearing properly?)

Any thoughts/experiences appreciated. Although frankly I'm skeptical this will ever be thoroughly explained.

It has come to my attention that people are starting to use peer-to-peer content delivery using WebRTC.

That is, the content of a website is first downloaded as normal by some users, and then other users instead of downloading data from the server, fetch the information from other users that are browsing the same website. This all is backed by some newish web standard that allows serverless communication between web browsers.

That's right, voat.co images, cached versions of comments, etc. could be delivered in a p2p fashion between users, cutting down costs, reducing the impact of DDOS and even improving loading speed in some cases.

There are some provider for this kind of technology that are mostly plug-and-play -- no modifications required: - http://swarmcdn.com/ - https://www.peer5.com/

You could also roll your own, which could have some advantages like caching comments as I said, and even making easier to add more advanced features like real-time chat, or video-conferencing between users.

Just so you know this is not some non-sense, even Netflix is also looking into this kind of technology. and some guys that were researching this kind of service where bough by Yahoo!

So what do you think?

Depends on what part of Reddit you're referring to.

  • The rampant hivemind homogenization of opinions and lack of interest in sincere discourse with opposing views could just be an artifact of human nature that will always come as a result of interactions on a large scale. It's seen in many aspects of online and real life communication from highschool cliques to comment sections on foodnetwork.com. Peer pressure is a crazy thing that we're all susceptible to whether we're cogniscient of it or not.

  • The disconnect between the paid staff of the website itself and the volunteer moderators that administer their communities is wholly a reddit issue and is hopefully something everyone can learn from and never repeat. The reddit team lost sight of who it is that truly creates the content that drives ad impressions. It's the users and the small groups of non-paid workers that try to keep the noise-to-signal ratio in check. As long as @Atko keep that in mind and focuses on maintaining transparency in how the site is administered, we'll be much better off.

So far things are starting out on good footing. Just maintain the ideals that behoove a service providing truly free (but legal) discourse on any (once again, legal) subject and listen to the users as problems arise.
